facts.text: The Australian Coal Association Research Program (ACARP) is the Australian coal industry's research fund; its project C26028 proposed two-tier testing of proximity detection systems, proving object detection before proving advisory or intervention action.
facts.quote: ACARP is the research fund of the Australian coal industry, and its project C26028 proposed a two-tier framework for testing proximity detection systems: first prove that the system detects objects, then prove that its advisory or intervention action works.

facts.text: ACARP is funded by a levy on coal production and commissions applied research for the Australian coal industry.
facts.quote: The Australian Coal Association Research Program (ACARP) is funded by a levy on coal production and commissions applied research for the industry.

facts.text: Mining3 delivered ACARP project C26028, a proximity detection system testing framework, in January 2021.
facts.quote: Project C26028, delivered by the research company Mining3 in January 2021, is a proximity detection system testing framework.

facts.text: ACARP C26028 tests object detection in Tier 1 and Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention in Tier 2.
facts.quote: Its two tiers are object detection first (Tier 1) and Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention second (Tier 2).

facts.text: The ACARP C26028 framework's baseline covers only limited choreographed test scenarios and ignores pre-existing site controls and complex, multi-variate dynamic vehicle interactions.
facts.quote: the baseline covers "limited choreographed test scenarios" and ignores "pre-existing site controls" and "complex, multi-variate dynamic vehicle interactions" [Chapter 1]

facts.text: The booklet identifies ACARP C26028, the Mining3 toolkit, NIOSH evaluations and the South African MOSH regime as industry-shared frameworks that provide comparability and credible independent evidence.
facts.quote: The booklet lists it, with the Mining3 toolkit, evaluations by the United States research institute NIOSH and the South African MOSH regime, among the industry-shared frameworks that give comparability and credible independent evidence [Chapter 1].

facts.text: The University of Queensland's ACARP project C24028, conducted in 2017 with follow-on work to 2019, used a modified haul-truck simulator to study proximity-advisory interface design.
facts.quote: Project C24028, by the University of Queensland (2017, with follow-on work to 2019), used a modified haul-truck simulator to study the design of proximity-advisory interfaces.

facts.text: In ACARP C24028's haul-truck simulator study, a richer schematic display reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time.
facts.quote: A richer schematic display reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time;

facts.text: ACARP C24028 explicitly identified an acceptable false alarm rate as a question requiring further research; the booklet states that the question remains open.
facts.quote: the project explicitly listed "acceptable false alarm rate" among the questions still requiring research [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The booklet recommends the ACARP two-tier structure for the collision mitigation project's physical test campaign: test detection first and intervention second, while recognizing that choreographed tests cannot replace site-specific, multi-variable dynamics.
facts.quote: detection first, intervention second, with the stated caution that choreographed tests cannot stand in for site-specific, multi-variable dynamics [Chapter 1].

facts.text: The booklet treats ACARP C24028's simulator study as its main off-road evidence that operator-in-the-loop testing works.
facts.quote: The simulator study is the booklet's main off-road evidence that operator-in-the-loop testing works
